questions.stem: Which of the following defines Zero Trust (ZT)?
questions.key: A set of cybersecurity paradigms that moves defenses from static, network-based perimeters to focus on users, assets and resources
distractors: An enterprise cybersecurity plan built on zero trust concepts, component relationships and access policies
The network infrastructure and operational policies in place as a product of the ZTA plan
A perimeter model that grants trust based on physical or network location
questions.explanation: Zero Trust is a set of cybersecurity paradigms; no implicit trust is granted based on physical or network location or on asset ownership.
why: That defines the Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), the plan.
That defines the ZT Enterprise, the result of the ZTA plan.
Zero Trust rejects implicit trust by location or ownership.

questions.stem: It is the enterprise cybersecurity plan built on zero trust concepts, component relationships, workflow planning and access policies.
distractors: Zero Trust (ZT)
Zero Trust Enterprise
Software-Defined Perimeter
questions.explanation: The slide separates the concept (ZT), the plan (ZTA) and the result (ZT Enterprise).
why: ZT is the concept of minimizing uncertainty in access decisions.
The ZT Enterprise is the resulting infrastructure and policies, not the plan.
SDP is a deployment approach, not the plan itself.

questions.stem: Which list contains the three principles of the Zero Trust Framework?
questions.key: Assume breach, verify explicitly, least privilege
distractors: Assume breach, verify explicitly, maximum access
Trust location, verify explicitly, least privilege
Assume breach, verify once, least privilege
questions.explanation: The framework slide gives three principles: assume breach, verify explicitly and least privilege.
why: Least privilege grants only the minimum access needed, not maximum access.
Trust is never granted implicitly by location.
Authentication and authorization are done per session, not once.

questions.stem: A unit grants access to a resource for one session only, so the next request must be authorized again. Which tenet does this describe?
questions.key: Access is granted on a per-session basis
distractors: Access is determined by dynamic policy (identity, device, behavior)
All communication is secured regardless of location
Authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced
questions.explanation: Tenet 3 says access is granted on a per-session basis.
why: Tenet 4 concerns policy built from identity, device and behavior.
Tenet 2 concerns securing communication wherever it occurs.
Tenet 6 concerns dynamic, strictly enforced authentication and authorization.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven tenets of Zero Trust?
questions.key: Devices inside the internal network are trusted by default
distractors: All data sources and computing services are resources
The enterprise monitors the integrity and posture of all assets
Collect and use data to continually improve security posture
questions.explanation: Zero Trust grants no implicit trust by location, so trusting internal devices by default is not a tenet.
why: Tenet 1 states all data sources and computing services are resources.
Tenet 5 states the enterprise monitors integrity and posture of all assets.
Tenet 7 states data is collected to continually improve posture.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)?
questions.key: It enables, monitors and terminates the connection between the subject and the resource
distractors: It grants, denies or revokes access using enterprise policy and a trust algorithm
It establishes or shuts down the communication path and issues session credentials
It is the enterprise resource sitting inside the implicit trust zone
questions.explanation: The PEP enforces: it enables, monitors and terminates the connection, and nothing reaches a resource except through a PEP.
why: That is the Policy Engine (PE), which decides.
That is the Policy Administrator (PA), which executes.
The resource is what the PEP protects; it is not the PEP.

questions.stem: A component establishes the communication path between a subject and a resource, issues session credentials and configures the PEP. Which component is this?
distractors: Policy Engine (PE)
Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)
Enterprise resource
questions.explanation: The PA executes the decision: it establishes or shuts down the path, issues session credentials and configures the PEP.
why: The PE makes the decision to grant, deny or revoke.
The PEP enforces the connection between subject and resource.
The resource is the asset being accessed.

questions.stem: It is the component that grants, denies or revokes access using enterprise policy and inputs fed to a trust algorithm.
distractors: Policy Administrator (PA)
Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)
Subject or system
questions.explanation: The PE decides, using enterprise policy plus inputs such as CDM, threat intelligence and logs in a trust algorithm.
why: The PA executes the decision by setting up or shutting down the path.
The PEP enforces the connection.
The subject or system is the party requesting access, not the decision-maker.

questions.stem: A unit places resources on protected segments behind gateways such as NGFWs and smart switches that act as PEPs. Which deployment approach is this?
distractors: Enhanced identity governance
Software-defined perimeter (SDP)
Reporting-only deployment
questions.explanation: In micro-segmentation, resources sit on protected segments behind gateways acting as PEPs, shielding them from unauthorized access and discovery.
why: Enhanced identity governance makes the identity of actors the key driver of policy.
SDP has the network infrastructure itself implement ZT, with the PA acting as network controller.
Reporting-only mode is a migration step, not a deployment approach.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the software-defined perimeter (SDP) approach?
questions.key: The network infrastructure itself implements ZT, with the PA acting as network controller reconfiguring paths per the PE's decisions
distractors: Identity of actors is the key driver of policy, with device and environment refining confidence
Resources are placed on protected segments behind gateways acting as PEPs
Stored traffic, scans and policies are protected with the most restrictive policies
questions.explanation: In SDP the infrastructure implements ZT through SDN or overlay networks; the PA acts as the network controller.
why: That defines enhanced identity governance.
That defines micro-segmentation.
That is guidance for the threat of storing network information, not a deployment approach.

questions.stem: A compromised or misconfigured PE approves access it should not. Which ZTA threat is this?
distractors: Denial of service / disruption
Stolen credentials / insider threat
Storage of network information
questions.explanation: The slide lists subversion of the decision process: a compromised or misconfigured PE/PA can approve what it should not.
why: Disruption concerns PE/PA/PEP becoming mission-critical choke points.
Stolen credentials concern abuse of valid accounts, addressed by MFA and contextual trust.
Storage of network information concerns stored traffic, scans and policies as reconnaissance material.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the lesson's guidance on the network visibility threat?
questions.key: Encrypted traffic cannot all be inspected, so analyze metadata and apply machine learning to spot malicious flows
distractors: Configure, monitor, log and audit all changes to the PE and PA
Replicate the PE, PA and PEP and host them in resilient, secured environments
Use MFA and contextual trust algorithms to detect abnormal access patterns
questions.explanation: For network visibility the lesson advises analyzing metadata and applying machine learning because encrypted traffic cannot all be inspected.
why: That is the answer to subversion of the decision process.
That is the answer to denial of service and disruption.
That is the answer to stolen credentials and insider threat.

questions.stem: Which list gives the first three steps of migrating to a ZTA, in order?
questions.key: Identify actors, identify assets, identify key processes
distractors: Identify assets, identify actors, identify key processes
Identify actors, identify key processes, formulate policies
Identify actors, identify assets, formulate policies
questions.explanation: The seven migration steps start with identify actors, identify assets and identify key processes, then formulate policies, identify solutions, deploy and monitor, and expand.
why: Actors are identified before assets.
Assets are inventoried before key processes are ranked.
Key processes are identified before policies are formulated.

questions.stem: A unit runs its new policies in reporting-only mode and tunes them against real traffic. Which migration step is this?
distractors: Identify solutions
Formulate policies
Expand the ZTA
questions.explanation: Step 6, Deploy and monitor, operates in reporting-only mode first and tunes policies against real traffic.
why: Identify solutions evaluates candidate tools against the workflow, assets and environment.
Formulate policies sets criteria or confidence-level weights for the workflow's resources.
Expand the ZTA refines and then takes on the next workflow.
